edits.source_excerpt: 3.1 For uniqueness, suppose $A=L_1L_1^*=L_2L_2^*$ are two such factorizations. Then $M:=L_2^{-1}L_1$ is lower triangular, and $MM^*=I$ because $L_2MM^*L_2^*=L_1L_1^*=L_2L_2^*$. A lower-triangular unitary matrix has zero strict-lower entries and diagonal entries of modulus $1$; since the diagonal of $M$ is the ratio of two positive real diagonals, each diagonal entry is also positive real, hence equals $1$. Therefore $M=I$ and $L_1=L_2$. [step 1.1, step 2.1, L2, L3, algebra]
edits.proposed_replacement: 3.1 For uniqueness, suppose $A=L_1L_1^*=L_2L_2^*$ are two such factorizations. By [L2] and [L5], both factors are invertible. Forward substitution in $L_2u=e_j$ gives $u_i=0$ for $i<j$ and $u_j=1/(L_2)_{jj}$, so $L_2^{-1}$ is lower triangular with reciprocal diagonal. Hence $M:=L_2^{-1}L_1$ is lower triangular with positive real diagonal, and $MM^*=I$ follows by multiplying $L_2MM^*L_2^*=L_1L_1^*=L_2L_2^*$ by the inverses. Its first row contains only $M_{11}$, so $MM^*=I$ gives $|M_{11}|=1$ and $M_{i1}\overline{M_{11}}=0$ for $i>1$. Removing this first row and column leaves a lower triangular block satisfying the same identity; induction gives zero strict-lower entries and unit-modulus diagonal throughout. Every diagonal entry is positive real, hence $1$, so $M=I$ and $L_1=L_2$. [step 1.1, step 2.1, L2, L3, L4, L5, algebra]
edits.reason: Make inverse-triangular and lower-unitary conclusions explicit; preserve exact existence/uniqueness claim.

edits.source_excerpt: 1.2 In the real case, for $(a,b)\ne(0,0)$ set $r=(a^2+b^2)^{1/2}$, $c=a/r$, and $s=b/r$. Then $c^2+s^2=1$ and $$ \begin{pmatrix}c&s\\-s&c\end{pmatrix}\binom{a}{b} =\binom{r}{0}. $$ In the complex case, if $a=0$ take $c=0$ and $s=b/|b|$; otherwise write $a=\phi|a|$ with $|\phi|=1$, set $r=(|a|^2+|b|^2)^{1/2}$, $c=|a|/r$, and $s=\phi\overline b/r$. Then $c^2+|s|^2=1$ and $$ \begin{pmatrix}c&s\\-\overline s&c\end{pmatrix}\binom{a}{b} =\binom{\phi r}{0}. $$ Thus a Givens transformation annihilates the second entry while preserving the Euclidean norm. [L1, algebra]

edits.source_excerpt: 2.1 If $z$ is already a scalar multiple of $e_1$, choose any Householder reflector fixing $e_1$: for $m=1$, $H=[-1]$ works; for $m>1$, take $v=e_2$, so $H_ve_1=e_1$. Otherwise set $\alpha:=e^{i\theta}\|z\|_2$, where $e^{i\theta}=z_1/|z_1|$ when $z_1\ne 0$ and $e^{i\theta}=1$ when $z_1=0$, and put $w:=z-\alpha e_1$, $v:=w/\|w\|_2$. Then $v^*z=(\|z\|_2^2-\overline\alpha z_1)/\|w\|_2=\|w\|_2/2$, so $H_vz=z-2v(v^*z)=z-w=\alpha e_1$. [L1, step 1.1, algebra]
edits.proposed_replacement: 2.1 If $z$ is already a scalar multiple of $e_1$, for $m=1$ take $H=[-1]$, which sends $z$ to $-z$ and preserves its norm; for $m>1$ take $v=e_2$, so $H_ve_1=e_1$ and $H_vz=z$. Both cases give the required first-coordinate alignment and output modulus. Otherwise put $\phi=z_1/|z_1|$ when $z_1\ne0$ and $\phi=1$ when $z_1=0$, and set $\alpha=\phi\|z\|_2$, $w=z-\alpha e_1$, $v=w/\|w\|_2$. Here $|\phi|=1$ and $\overline\alpha z_1=\|z\|_2|z_1|$ is real, so $\|w\|_2^2=2(\|z\|_2^2-\overline\alpha z_1)$ and $v^*z=(\|z\|_2^2-\overline\alpha z_1)/\|w\|_2=\|w\|_2/2$. Thus $H_vz=z-2v(v^*z)=z-w=\alpha e_1$. For real $z$ this selects real $\phi,w,v$, so the reflector is real. [L1, step 1.1, algebra]

edits.source_excerpt:
Use a left Givens factor $L(a,b)$ that sends the column pair $(a,b)^T$ to
$(\gamma,0)^T$, with $|\gamma|=(|a|^2+|b|^2)^{1/2}$; if $a=b=0$, use the
identity. Use a right Givens factor $R(a,b)$ that sends the row pair $(a,b)$ to
$(0,\eta)$, with $|\eta|=(|a|^2+|b|^2)^{1/2}$; if $a=b=0$, use the identity.
These factors are obtained from
[[def-real-and-complex-givens-transformations]] and are orthogonal over
$\mathbb R$ or unitary over $\mathbb C$.
edits.proposed_replacement:
For a target pair $(a,b)$, define the left factor $L(a,b)$ deterministically. Use $I_2$ if $a=b=0$. Otherwise put $r=(|a|^2+|b|^2)^{1/2}$ and $L=\begin{pmatrix}c&s\\-\overline s&c\end{pmatrix}$. Over $\mathbb R$, take $c=a/r$, $s=b/r$. Over $\mathbb C$, if $a=0$ take $c=0$, $s=\overline b/|b|$; otherwise take $\phi=a/|a|$, $c=|a|/r$, $s=\phi\overline b/r$. Thus $L(a,b)(a,b)^T=(\gamma,0)^T$ with $|\gamma|=r$. Set $J=\begin{pmatrix}0&1\\1&0\end{pmatrix}$ and define the right factor
$$R(a,b)=J L(\overline b,\overline a)^*J.$$
Then $(a,b)R(a,b)=(0,\eta)$ with $|\eta|=r$; the zero pair again uses identity. These factors are real orthogonal over $\mathbb R$ or unitary over $\mathbb C$, as direct multiplication shows in [[thm-householder-reflectors-and-givens-transformations-are-unitary-and-annihilate-targeted-entries]]; the right identity follows by taking adjoints of the left annihilation of $(\overline b,\overline a)^T$ and reversing the coordinates. Use their identity embeddings on the two rows or columns specified by each step below.
edits.reason: Deterministic real/complex selectors and exact correct row-first orientation; preserve all index loops/output contract.
